heading: Placement practice
workedExample: For 2x+3=13, subtract 3 from both sides to get 2x=10, then divide by 2: x=5. Checking gives 2(5)+3=13.
questions: Solve 3x+7=22 and check the result in the original equation.
A location moves from (1,2) to (4,8). Find its change in each coordinate and the slope joining the points.
Solve y=x+1 and y=7-x. Check the intersection in both rules.
answers: Horizontal change is 3 and vertical change is 6; slope=6/3=2.

heading: Properties practice
workedExample: Distribute 3 across (x+2) to obtain 3x+6. Adding -6 to each side of 3(x+2)=15 gives 3x=9 and x=3; both original sides equal 15.
questions: Expand 4(x-3) and explain which factors multiply the constant.
Simplify 2x+5+3x-2 by grouping like terms. Verify at x=-1.
Decide whether x=2 solves 3x+4=13. Show both sides.
answers: 4x-12: the factor 4 multiplies both x and -3.
5x+3. At x=-1 the original is -2+5-3-2=-2, matching -5+3=-2.
It does not: 3(2)+4=10, while the right side is 13. The actual solution is x=3.

heading: Single-step practice
workedExample: For -3x=18, divide both sides by -3: x=-6. Multiplication checks -3(-6)=18.
questions: Solve x-7=-12 and verify.
Solve -4x=20 and verify.
Solve x/5=-3 and verify; explain why multiplication undoes division.
answers: Divide by -4: x=-5, and -4(-5)=20.
Multiply both sides by 5: x=-15; -15/5=-3. Multiplying by the nonzero divisor reverses the division.

heading: Multi-step practice
workedExample: Solve 2(x+3)=x+11: distribute to get 2x+6=x+11, subtract x and 6, and obtain x=5. Both sides are 16.
questions: Solve 3(x-2)+4=2x+9. Verify in the original equation.
Classify 2(x+1)=2x+2 as one solution, no solution or all real numbers. Explain.
Classify 2(x+1)=2x+5 in the same way. Explain why dividing by a zero coefficient cannot find a solution.
answers: 3x-2=2x+9 gives x=11; the original sides are 31.
All real numbers: distribution gives the identity 2x+2=2x+2.
No solution: subtracting 2x gives 2=5. The resulting 0x=3 is impossible; division by zero is undefined.

heading: First check-in practice
workedExample: A fee of $8 plus $3 per visit is C=8+3v. At v=4, C=20 dollars; (4,20) satisfies the equation.
questions: A booth charges $12 plus $4 per item. How many items give a total of $36?
A club has a $50 budget and pays $8 per hour. Find the largest whole number of hours it can buy.
Solve 5-2x=17. Explain why the solution may be negative even though the right side is positive.
answers: 8h<=50 gives h<=6.25. The largest whole number is 6: $48 fits, while 7 hours cost $56.
-2x=12, so x=-6; 5-2(-6)=17. Multiplying two negative numbers contributes +12.

module: AA6 Slope and Rate of Change
heading: Slope practice
workedExample: Between (1,3) and (4,9), slope=(9-3)/(4-1)=2. The line y=2x+1 contains both points.
questions: Find the slope from (-2,5) to (2,-3). Reverse both point orders and compare.
Find the slopes of the lines through (3,-1),(3,4) and through (-2,7),(5,7). Explain each.
A tank holds 50 liters at minute 2 and 35 liters at minute 5, with a constant drain rate. Find the rate and predict minute 6.
answers: (-3-5)/(2-(-2))=-8/4=-2; reversing both differences gives 8/(-4)=-2.
The first is vertical x=3 and has undefined slope because its horizontal change is zero. The second is horizontal y=7 with slope 0.
(35-50)/(5-2)=-5 liters per minute. Continuing that constant rate gives 30 liters at minute 6.

module: AA7 Module Project: Community Data Analysis (with Davin Lee)
heading: Community data practice
workedExample: Fictional records (month,visits)=(1,10),(2,14),(3,18) have rate 4 visits per month and rule v=4m+6. Substituting m=1,2,3 reproduces the data.
questions: For fictional records (1,8),(2,11),(3,14),(4,17), find the rate and a matching linear rule.
Another fictional series is (1,8),(2,11),(3,15),(4,20). Calculate its three successive rates. Does one exact linear rule match all four points?
Use the first series to predict month 5 under continued linear growth. Explain whether the data alone show that a library program caused the increase.
answers: Each monthly change is 3; v=3m+5 matches all four records.
Rates are 3,4,5 visits per month. They vary, so one exact straight line cannot contain all four points.
v(5)=20 visits if the pattern continues. A pattern in these fictional observations does not establish a cause.

heading: Slope-intercept practice
workedExample: In y=-2x+7, -2 is the output change per unit of input and 7 is the value at x=0. Points (0,7) and (2,3) check both features.
questions: Write the line with slope 3 and y-intercept -4. Give its points at x=0 and x=2.
A taxi fare is F=5+2d dollars for d>=0 kilometers. Interpret both constants and find the fare at d=7.
A line contains (0,-1) and (4,7). Find its slope-intercept equation and check both points.
answers: The fixed fee is $5 and the rate is $2 per kilometer. F(7)=19 dollars.
Slope=(7-(-1))/4=2 and intercept=-1, so y=2x-1; it gives -1 at 0 and 7 at 4.

heading: Point-slope practice
workedExample: A line of slope 2 through (3,-1) has y+1=2(x-3), equivalently y=2x-7. Substitution of (3,-1) gives 0=0.
questions: Write point-slope and slope-intercept equations for slope -3 through (2,5).
Find a line through (-1,4) and (3,-4) in both forms. Verify both points.
Write the line through (4,-2) parallel to y=x/2+6. Compare the two intercepts.
answers: Slope=-8/4=-2; y-4=-2(x+1), hence y=-2x+2. At x=-1 it gives 4; at x=3 it gives -4.
y+2=(x-4)/2, so y=x/2-4. The slopes agree and the intercepts -4 and 6 differ.

heading: Inequality practice
workedExample: For -2x<6, division by -2 reverses the inequality: x>-3. The boundary -3 is excluded; x=0 passes and x=-4 fails.
questions: Solve -3x+6<=15 and test the boundary and one point on each side.
Describe and sketch y>2x-1, including the boundary line, its inclusion and the shaded side. Test (0,0).
A $24 budget buys $5 tickets after a fixed $4 fee. Find the allowed nonnegative whole-number ticket counts.
answers: -3x<=9 gives x>=-3. At -3 the left side is 15, at 0 it is 6, and at -4 it is 18.
Use a dashed y=2x-1 line and shade above it; boundary points are excluded. (0,0) passes because 0>-1.
4+5n<=24 gives n<=4; with the stated domain, n can be 0,1,2,3,4.

module: AA12 Solving Linear Systems by Graphing
heading: Graphing systems practice
workedExample: The lines y=x+1 and y=-x+5 cross at (2,3). A table around x=2 helps locate the crossing; substitution verifies 3=2+1 and 3=-2+5.
questions: Graph y=2x and y=-x+6 using at least two points per line. Find and verify their intersection.
Classify y=2x+1 and y=2x-3. Explain why extending the graph will not produce an intersection.
Classify y=3x-2 and 2y=6x-4. Give two shared points and explain the number of solutions.
answers: For y=2x, use (0,0),(2,4); for y=-x+6, use (0,6),(2,4). The intersection is (2,4), satisfying both.
No solution: equal slopes and distinct intercepts give parallel lines.
Infinitely many solutions: dividing the second equation by 2 yields the first. Both contain (0,-2) and (1,1).

module: AA13 Solving Linear Systems by Substitution
heading: Substitution practice
workedExample: For y=2x+1 and x+y=10, replace y to get x+2x+1=10. Thus x=3 and y=7; 7=2(3)+1 and 3+7=10.
questions: Solve y=3x-2 and 2x+y=13 by substitution. Check both equations.
Solve x=2y+1 and 3x-y=13. Check both equations.
One large and one small ticket cost $11; two large and three small tickets cost $27. Find both positive prices using substitution.
answers: 5x-2=13 gives x=3,y=7. Checks: 7=9-2 and 6+7=13.
Let L+S=11 and 2L+3S=27. Substituting L=11-S gives S=5 dollars, L=6 dollars; 6+5=11 and 12+15=27.

module: AA14 Solving Linear Systems by Elimination
heading: Elimination practice
workedExample: Add 2x+y=7 and 3x-y=8 to eliminate y: 5x=15, so x=3 and y=1. The original left sides are 7 and 8.
questions: Solve 2x+3y=12 and 2x-y=4 by subtracting entire equations. Verify.
Solve 3x+2y=12 and 2x-3y=-5 by scaling and adding. Verify.
A total of 20 tickets earns $130. Adult tickets cost $8 and child tickets $5. Find each count with elimination and check the whole-number constraints.
answers: Subtracting gives 4y=8, so y=2 and x=3. Checks: 6+6=12 and 6-2=4.
Scale by 3 and 2: 9x+6y=36 and 4x-6y=-10. Then 13x=26, x=2,y=3. Checks: 6+6=12 and 4-9=-5.
a+c=20 and 8a+5c=130. Subtract 5(a+c)=100 to get 3a=30; a=10,c=10. Counts total 20 and revenue is 80+50=130 dollars.

heading: Capstone review practice
workedExample: Two fees A=10+3h and B=4+5h are equal when 10+3h=4+5h. Thus h=3 and each costs $19; this checks the intersection and its units.
questions: For plans A=12+2h and B=6+4h, h>=0 hours, find when their costs match and which is cheaper after that point.
An account begins with $60 and loses $7 per week. For how many whole weeks is its balance at least $25?
A line joins (1,5) and (4,11). Give its equation in two forms and explain how a table of three points could check it.
answers: Equality at h=3 hours and $18. For h>3, A is cheaper because B's hourly rate is larger; the cost difference B-A=2h-6 is positive.
60-7w>=25 gives w<=5. With w>=0 whole, the allowed values are 0 through 5; week 5 has $25 and week 6 has $18.
Slope=6/3=2; y-5=2(x-1) and y=2x+3. The points (1,5),(2,7),(4,11) satisfy the rule; equal input steps have equal output changes.

heading: Signed division
flawed: Divide both sides by 5 to obtain x=6, because dividing removes the coefficient.
questions: Identify the first invalid equality and the coefficient that must be removed.
Solve the equation correctly, showing the operation on both sides.
Check both x=6 and the corrected value in the original equation.
answers: Dividing by 5 gives -x=6, not x=6. The full coefficient is -5.
Divide by -5 to get x=-6.
At 6 the left side is -30, which fails. At -6 it is 30, which equals the right side.

module: AA3 Module Project: Movie Star Status (with Maddie Van Beek)
heading: Film budget units
given: A fictional production pays $150 per producer-hour, $25 per prop and $32.50 per marketing-hour. It books 4 producer-hours, buys 8 props and books 6 marketing-hours. A separate editing bill is $400. The total budget is $1,500.
flawed: The total is 150+25+32.50+400=$607.50, leaving $892.50 for other work.
questions: Explain why adding the three rates directly gives an incorrect cost.
Find the actual cost of each category and the total.
Find the remaining budget and the largest extra whole-number producer-hours it can cover if nothing else changes.
answers: Each unit rate must be multiplied by its matching quantity before adding dollar amounts.
Production costs 150(4)=600, props 25(8)=200, marketing 32.50(6)=195 and editing 400 dollars. Total=$1,395.
Remaining=$105. An extra producer-hour costs $150, so the budget allows zero extra whole producer-hours; $105/150=0.7 is not a whole hour.

heading: Strict budget threshold
given: A campaign starts with $150 and spends $20 after each completed day. It places an order only when the remaining amount is strictly below $30. Let d be the nonnegative whole-number completed days.
flawed: 150-20d<30 gives -20d<-120, so d<6. The first order is on day 1.
questions: Find the first incorrect inequality transformation.
Solve the inequality and identify the first qualifying whole-number day.
Evaluate the balance on days 5,6 and 7 to test the strict threshold.
answers: Division by -20 reverses the inequality; d must be greater than 6.
d>6, so the first qualifying whole-number day is 7.
Balances are $50,$30,$10. Day 6 is exactly the threshold and fails a strict 'below' condition; day 7 qualifies.

module: AA6 Slope and Rate of Change
heading: Matching slope differences
given: A line contains A=(-2,5) and B=(2,-3).
flawed: The slope is (5-(-3))/(2-(-2))=8/4=2, so the line rises as x increases.
questions: Identify which coordinate order is inconsistent.
Find the correct slope and an equation for the line.
Check both given points and state whether the line rises or falls from left to right.
answers: The numerator uses A minus B but the denominator uses B minus A. Both differences must use the same order.
At -2 the rule gives 5; at 2 it gives -3. The negative slope means the line falls as x increases.

heading: Fixed fees and rates
given: A rental charges a fixed $12 plus $3 per hour for h>=0. Let C be total dollars.
flawed: C=12h+3. Five hours cost $63, and the graph's slope is $12 per hour.
questions: Identify the swapped meanings of the two constants.
Write the correct rule and calculate the costs at h=0 and h=5.
Give two graph points and use them to recover the hourly rate.
answers: 12 is the starting fee, while 3 is dollars per hour.
C=12+3h. The costs are $12 at zero hours and $27 at five hours.
(0,12) and (5,27) give slope (27-12)/(5-0)=3 dollars per hour.

heading: Negative point coordinates
given: Find the line with slope 2 through (-3,4).
flawed: Point-slope form is y-4=2(x-3), so y=2x-2.
questions: Identify the sign error in substituting the point.
Write the corrected point-slope and slope-intercept forms.
Substitute (-3,4) into both proposed lines to compare their validity.
answers: The x-coordinate is -3, so x-x1 is x-(-3)=x+3.
The flawed rule gives -8 at x=-3; the corrected rule gives 4. Only the corrected line contains the supplied point.

heading: Boundary and shading
given: Graph y<=-x+4 on a coordinate plane.
flawed: Draw a dashed boundary because this is an inequality, and shade above the line because y is on the left.
questions: Explain the correct boundary style and whether (0,4) belongs to the solution.
Use (0,0) as a test point to choose the shaded side.
Give one point outside the solution and verify it algebraically.
answers: The <= sign includes equality, so the line is solid and (0,4) belongs.
0<=4 is true, so shade the half-plane containing (0,0), below the boundary.
(0,5) fails because 5<=4 is false.

module: AA11 Module Project: Predicting Avalanches (with Ruby Lee)
heading: Listed observations and strict thresholds
given: Use only this fictional classroom table: day 2 has 60%, day 4 has 40%, and day 5 has 30%. The question asks for the first listed day below 40%; the table supplies no values between those days.
flawed: Day 4 is below the threshold because 40% is low enough. The probability drops by exactly 10 percentage points every day, so day 3 must have been 50%.
questions: Identify the error in the threshold comparison.
Find the first qualifying listed day and calculate the average change from day 2 to day 4.
Explain which statement about day 3 needs an additional assumption. Keep the conclusion limited to the supplied mathematical model.
answers: 40% equals the threshold; it is not strictly below 40%.
Day 5 is the first listed qualifying day. Average change from day 2 to day 4 is (40-60)/(4-2)=-10 percentage points per day.
A day-3 value of 50% requires linear interpolation. An interval average alone does not prove a constant daily change or describe conditions beyond this fictional table.

heading: Parallel through a given point
given: Find the line through (-1,1) parallel to y=-4x+6.
flawed: Use y=-4x+6 because parallel lines have the same equation. The given point must lie on it.
questions: Separate the required shared feature from the feature that can differ.
Find the correct new intercept and equation.
Check the point and explain whether the two distinct lines intersect.
answers: Parallel nonvertical lines share their slope; their intercepts can differ.
1=-4(-1)+b gives b=-3. The new equation is y=-4x-3.
At x=-1 the new line gives 1; the old gives 10. Equal slopes with different intercepts mean no intersection.

module: AA12 Solving Linear Systems by Graphing
heading: One constraint is insufficient
given: Find the intersection of y=2x+1 and y=-x+7.
flawed: (1,3) solves y=2x+1, so it is the system's solution. No further check is necessary.
questions: Test the proposed pair in each original rule.
Find the actual intersection by equating the outputs, then locate it on a sketch.
Explain why solving one line cannot establish a system's solution.
answers: 3=2(1)+1 is true, but 3=-1+7 is false because the right side is 6.
2x+1=-x+7 gives x=2,y=5. Both rules contain (2,5).
A system requires both constraints simultaneously. A point on just one line need not lie on the other.

module: AA13 Solving Linear Systems by Substitution
heading: Substituting the whole expression
flawed: Replace y by 2x but leave out the -3, giving 6x=15 and x=2.5. Then y=2, so the pair is (2.5,2).
questions: Identify the missing part of the substitution.
Solve using the entire expression and recover both coordinates.
Check the flawed pair and corrected pair in both original equations.
answers: The replacement for y is the entire expression 2x-3.
The flawed pair satisfies y=2x-3 but 4(2.5)+2=12, not 15. For (3,3), 3=6-3 and 12+3=15.

module: AA15 Module Project: Cytogenetics Quest (with Dr. Renu Bajaj)
heading: Two-type inventory
given: A fictional classroom inventory has 46 specimens of two types. The first type costs 2 tokens per specimen and the second costs 3. Total cost is 118 tokens. Let x and y be the two nonnegative whole-number counts.
flawed: x+y=46 and 2x+3y=118. Subtract twice the first equation to obtain y=118-46=72.
questions: Identify the incorrect subtraction, including the scaled constant.
Solve for both counts by elimination.
Check both the count and cost constraints and explain why the negative count implied by y=72 is invalid.
answers: Twice the first equation is 2x+2y=92, so the right-side difference is 118-92.
y=26 and x=20.
20+26=46 and 2(20)+3(26)=118. If y were 72, x would be -26, violating the stated domain and cost equation.

module: AA16 Module Project: Battle of the Publications (with Konstantin Kaganovsky)
heading: Publication quota model
given: In a fictional publication model, Lab A starts with 12 papers and adds 3 per month. Lab B starts with 6 and adds 5 per month. Let m>=0 be elapsed months, with constant rates.
flawed: Use A=12m+3 and B=6m+5. The labs tie after 1/3 month because starting totals are the slopes.
questions: Correct the meaning and placement of the starting totals and monthly rates.
Find when the labs have equal totals and verify both values.
Find the first whole-number month with B>A and explain how the rate difference affects the comparison.
answers: A=12+3m and B=6+5m; starting totals are the intercepts.
12+3m=6+5m gives m=3 months and 21 papers for each lab.
B-A=2m-6, so B>A when m>3. The first whole-number month is 4; B gains two more papers per month than A.

heading: Comparing plans over a domain
given: A presentation compares fees A=20+2n and B=5+5n dollars for a nonnegative whole-number count n of visits.
flawed: Plan B starts cheaper, so it is always cheaper. Testing n=0 proves the conclusion for every visit count.
questions: Explain why one input cannot settle the comparison for the whole domain.
Find the equal-cost visit count and determine the cheaper plan on either side.
Test n=2 and n=8 and state a precise conclusion suitable for the presentation.
answers: The two rates differ, so the cost difference changes with the input.
20+2n=5+5n gives n=5 and a cost of $30. B is cheaper for n<5 and A for n>5.
At 2 visits, A=$24 and B=$15; at 8, A=$36 and B=$45. B is cheaper for 0 through 4 visits, both tie at 5, and A is cheaper for 6 or more visits.
